assessments.reasoning: PDF page 270 addresses Visual Basic 6.0 users, describes earlier Visual Basic versions, and identifies Visual Basic .NET 2002 as the point from which the newer application target and CLR-oriented language changes apply. This directly supports the historical boundary represented by the index display name.

challenge.method: Compared the migration guide's date boundary with Microsoft's release history (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/visual-basic/whats-new/) and challenged potential identities based on the Visual Basic name, Visual Studio branding, and Windows application targets.
challenge.results: Release history names 2002 as the first Visual Basic .NET release and places 2003 and 2005 later. Both sides can address Windows client applications, so the target alone fails as an identity test. The candidate uses the documented transition and an editorial parenthetical.

limitations: The display name represents the pre-.NET Visual Basic line in the migration account. The evidence establishes neither a release inventory nor a general compatibility promise.
